text.p: A sharp downward reaction by the U.S. Treasury and Wall Street stock markets to a much stronger than expected Chicago purchasing managers index helped the dollar drift lower in late European business.

The August index came in a 60.0, much stronger than the 51.9 expected by the market and July's 51.2. A 1.8-percent rise in July factory orders did not help the situation though a robust figure had been expected after a strong durable good figure last Friday.
The dollar was at 1.4784/92 marks, over half a pfennig down from the days high. It closed on Thursday at 1.4810/15.

The dollar held steadier on the yen at a late 108.57/67, up slightly from an early 108.30/35 and Thursday's 108.45/55. "The data will add to the concerns over the strength of the U.S. economy," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.
"The dollar has failed to gain much ground so far, and the upside may be limited if the market starts to believe that the Fed is behind the curve."
Dealers said the bond and stock market action was probably exaggerated by the thin trading conditions ahead of the long U.S. Labor Day holiday weekend.
The strong Chicago PM index got analysts rising their forecasts for the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) due on Tuesday.

Comments from Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer that U.S. fundamentals should allow a slightly higher dollar helped underpin the U.S. currency earlier today, and got some in the market talking about possible dollar/mark intervention. The Bundesbank's dramatic repo cut has failed to dent the mighty mark and with the crucial European budget season coming up the case for concerted action on the forex market becomes more attractive, said Paribas forex strategist Nick Parsons.

Parsons noted that the Bundesbank's intervention on August 15 last year boosted the dollar from 1.4365 to 1.4815 within 24 hours and underlined the German central bank's determination to boost German competitiveness. "Similar action now, we believe, would be equally successful, underpinning the dollar, removing pressure from the French franc and lira, and giving a further boost to domestic business confidence," Parsons said.
"With the Bundesbank's fondness for intervention on or around market holiday's, Labor Day may be busier than the market expects."
The mark spent most of the session easier on the European crosses but late in the session began to re-assert itself.

The French franc got to 3.4197 per mark high as traders covered shorts ahead of Sunday's meeting in Bonn between French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl. But in late business is was back a 3.4213/18.
The Finnish markka was boosted by talk of its possible entry into the Exchange Rate Mechanism. It hit a 3.0170 per mark high compared with Thursday's 3.0225/55.
The Swiss franc fell sharply on comments from the Swiss National Bank's chief economist Georg Rich.
Rich said the franc was ripe for correction and the SNB "could contribute to trigger such developments by adjusting monetary policy".
It sank to a session low of 81.17 centimes per mark before recovering to 81.04/07, down from Thursday's 80.85/87.
